analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, military and federal plans, and private insurers to cover medically necessary food for serious digestive and metabolic disorders.
analysis.headline: The bill had 32 cosponsors, including 12 Republicans, but was referred to four House committees and never received a hearing or a vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: People with inherited metabolic disorders, severe food allergies, short bowel syndrome, Crohn's disease, and similar conditions often need specially formulated foods and vitamins to survive or grow. Insurance usually treats those products as groceries, not medicine, so families pay out of pocket and some patients end up hospitalized or worse. This bill would have written those products into the covered benefits of Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, federal employee plans, and all private health insurance.
analysis.who_benefits: Families of children and adults whose digestive or inherited metabolic disorders require medically necessary food — amino acid formulas, low-protein foods, and the equipment to deliver them. The bill's own findings note that without coverage, patients suffer hospitalization, impaired growth, nutrient deficiencies, and even death, and that the cost is often an insurmountable financial burden for families. Federal employees and military families would also get the coverage, and Medicare beneficiaries would pay only the standard 20% coinsurance.

how_it_helps.text: Adds medically necessary food and delivery equipment as a covered benefit under Medicare, paying 80% of the cost under the standard fee schedule, and adds medically necessary vitamins as a covered Part D drug [S3].

Makes medically necessary food and vitamins a mandatory Medicaid benefit for all states and adds the same coverage to CHIP, so low-income children get it without waiting on state-by-state decisions [S3].
Extends coverage to TRICARE for military families, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and all group and individual private health insurance plans nationwide [S3].

Limits the mandate to prescription-grade formulated products used under ongoing medical supervision — it excludes weight-loss foods, gluten-free foods marketed for celiac disease, and diabetes foods — keeping the scope tied to diagnosed disorders [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and government health programs bear the cost of the new coverage, which is passed on to policyholders through premiums and to taxpayers through federal spending. Specialty medical food manufacturers gain a guaranteed nationwide payer for their products.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a new nationwide mandate on every group and individual health insurance plan, which would raise premiums for all policyholders and add unquantified federal spending to Medicare and Medicaid; the bill contains no cost estimate or financing mechanism [S3].

Coverage is limited to specially formulated commercial products and excludes ordinary foods, so even families who benefit would still face the cost of the regular-food part of a therapeutic diet, and specialty food manufacturers would gain a federally guaranteed market [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the affected families, the benefit is direct and severe: insurance would finally pay for food that doctors prescribe as medical treatment, potentially preventing hospitalizations and lifelong harm. The cost is real but spread thin — modestly higher premiums and government health spending across everyone — and the narrow, diagnosis-based definition keeps the mandate from becoming a broad food subsidy. The main design weakness is the lack of any cost estimate, which is the kind of gap that committee scrutiny is supposed to address; this bill never received that scrutiny.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in four House committees after introduction — a referral to Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Armed Services, and Oversight and Government Reform — and none of them ever scheduled a hearing or a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 22, 2017 by Rep. John Delaney with Reps. Herrera Beutler, Capuano, and Lynch as original cosponsors, and was referred the same day to four House committees [S5].

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee in May and June 2017 and to the Armed Services Military Personnel Subcommittee in June 2017, but no committee or subcommittee ever took further action [S5].
It attracted 32 cosponsors — 12 Republicans and 20 Democrats — yet no markup, hearing, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers are better off: the bill died before it could require them to cover prescription foods, so no new mandate, premium pressure, or government spending was created, and affected families kept paying out of pocket.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was genuinely bipartisan — 12 Republicans and 20 Democrats — and no one publicly opposed the bill; it died from committee inaction, not from a recorded partisan vote.

industries.note: The bill would have required every private plan to cover prescription-grade medical food, adding a benefit insurers currently avoid by classifying it as ordinary groceries. Their interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the families who need the coverage.

industries.industry: Specialty medical food and formula manufacturers
industries.note: Mandatory coverage would have given their formulated products — amino acid preparations and low-protein foods — a guaranteed payer across Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurance. Because the bill excludes ordinary foods, the benefit is structured to flow through their commercial products.

industries.industry: Federal and state taxpayers and Medicare/Medicaid budgets
industries.note: Medicaid would have become a mandatory benefit for all states, adding federal and state spending with no offset. For patients on public programs, that same spending is the help they need.
